result.final_text:
## What this letter says

You fell at home and hit your head on 14 October 2026. You did not lose consciousness (pass out).

Your right hip X-ray showed no fracture (broken bone). Tests show you did not have any bleeding inside your head. These are good results.

The doctors found that your blood pressure drops a lot when you stand up. This is called postural hypotension (blood pressure drops on standing). Your blood pressure when lying down was 142/80. When you stood up, it dropped to 108/66.

One of your medicines, amlodipine, may be causing this blood pressure drop. The doctors want you to stop taking it.

## What you need to do

1. Stop taking amlodipine 10 mg.
2. Stand up slowly. Sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before standing.
3. Continue all your other medicines.
4. You have been referred to the Falls Prevention Clinic. They will write to you with an appointment.
5. Your GP will recheck your lying and standing blood pressure in 4 weeks.

## Dates and medicines

Seen at Emergency Department: 14 October 2026

Amlodipine 10 mg
- Stop taking this medicine
- It may be causing your blood pressure to drop when standing

## Questions to ask your doctor

1. Is it safe to stop amlodipine, or should I reduce it slowly?
2. Will I get a different blood pressure medicine to replace it?
3. What should I do if I feel dizzy or faint?
4. How long will the Falls Prevention Clinic take to arrange an appointment?

## When to get urgent help

If you develop a worsening headache, vomiting, confusion or drowsiness in the next few days, call 999 or go to A&E.

If you are worried and it is not an emergency, call NHS 111. In an emergency, call 999.

---
*This explanation was made by a computer program to help you read your letter. It may contain mistakes. It does not replace your doctor, nurse or pharmacist. Always follow the letter and ask them if anything is unclear.*

problems.letter_says: The letter describes the patient's fall and separately reports that postural hypotension (blood pressure drop when standing from 142/80 to 108/66) was found, but does not state or imply that the postural hypotension caused the fall.
problems.why: The explanation adds a causal inference connecting the postural hypotension to the fall. While this may be clinically reasonable, the letter does not make this connection explicit.
